structure.text: What counts as serendipity: are its parts (surprise, agency, value) present, what was the search state, which type is it, and is it more than luck or targeted search?
What triggers it: an anomaly, an error, a chance meeting, a passing remark, an unsought offer, or a market signal?
What background (prior knowledge, a problem in mind, contacts) and which mechanisms (noticing, connecting, acting, changing plans) turn the trigger into an opportunity?
What role does it play in the venture (founding, redirecting, advancing it), and what outcomes follow: a product, a market, growth, or nothing?
Which conditions make it more or less likely to occur and be acted on: seeking out chance, cheap trials, loose plans, or scarce resources?
How do founders account for it afterwards: as luck, as luck plus effort, as clear only in hindsight, or retold as planned?

level1.name: Parts of serendipity
level1.sq_text: What counts as serendipity: are its parts (surprise, agency, value) present, what was the search state, which type is it, and is it more than luck or targeted search?

pick_one.name: Search state
pick_one.asks: What was the founder doing when it happened?

options.label: Not looking at all
options.captures: The founder was not looking for a business or an idea. A need and a way to meet it turned up together in everyday life, and they saw an opportunity.
options.papers: Busch and Grimes (2023); Bhave (1994); Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017); + 4 more

options.label: Open to any business
options.captures: The founder wanted to start or grow a business but had no specific idea, and a suitable opportunity came along by chance (Mirvahedi and Morrish's 'entrepreneurial serendipity').

options.label: Searching for something specific
options.captures: When the unexpected event happened, the founder was already looking for something: an idea, a solution, customers or a way forward. Needed for the narrow verdict (Dew 2009).
options.papers: Dew (2009); Balzano (2022); McFarlane and Carter (2016); + 3 more

codes.label: Surprise
codes.captures: Something happened that the founder did not expect, plan or intend.
codes.papers: Busch (2024); Austin et al. (2012); Balzano (2022); + 2 more

codes.label: Agency: acted on it
codes.captures: The founder did something with the unexpected event: followed it up, tried it, or built on it. Without this, it is luck, not serendipity.
codes.papers: Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); Fultz and Hmieleski (2021); Cunha et al. (2015); + 6 more

codes.label: Value
codes.captures: The unexpected event led to something the founder sees as worth having: an idea, customer, product, partner or turning point.
codes.papers: Reijonen and Heroum (2026); Merton and Barber (2004); Pease et al. (2013); + 7 more

level1.name: Trigger
level1.sq_text: What triggers it: an anomaly, an error, a chance meeting, a passing remark, an unsought offer, or a market signal?

codes.label: Something odd was noticed
codes.captures: The founder noticed something strange or contrary to expectation, and it led to an idea or a new direction.
codes.papers: Cunha et al. (2010); Merton and Barber (2004); Andel (1994); + 10 more

codes.label: A mistake or accident
codes.captures: An error, slip, malfunction or accident produced something unexpected that turned out to be useful.
codes.papers: McFarlane and Carter (2016); Balzano (2022); Copeland et al. (2023); + 4 more

codes.label: A chance meeting
codes.captures: An unplanned meeting with a person led to a partner, co-founder, customer, investor or opportunity.
codes.papers: Dew (2009); Copeland et al. (2023); Brown (2005); + 14 more

codes.label: A passing remark
codes.captures: A casual comment, question or piece of feedback from someone else revealed a possibility the founder had not seen.
codes.papers: Baker et al. (2003); Reinsberger et al. (2026); Hargadon and Sutton (1997); + 12 more

codes.label: An unasked-for offer or request
codes.captures: Someone approached the founder, unsought, with an offer, order, invitation or unusual request, and this started or changed the venture.
codes.papers: Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017); Baker et al. (2003); Kirtley and O'Mahony (2023); + 4 more

codes.label: An unexpected market signal
codes.captures: Customers or users responded in a way the founder did not expect: surprising demand, unexpected uses, or feedback showing the plan was wrong.
codes.papers: Garud et al. (2018); Shah and Tripsas (2007); Denrell et al. (2015); + 1 more

codes.label: An outside crisis or disaster (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: A sudden, large event outside the venture, such as a recession, a pandemic or a natural disaster, opened an opportunity or threatened the venture.
codes.papers: Garud and Karnøe (2003); Ma (2002); Merton and Barber (2004); + 3 more

codes.label: A change in technology, rules or platforms (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: Something outside the founder's control changed: a technology matured, a rule changed, or a platform or supplier the venture relied on changed its policy, algorithm or product. It opened a door or caused a setback.
codes.papers: Ma (2002); Cattani (2005); Davidsson (2015); + 6 more

codes.label: Came across information by chance (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: While doing something else, the founder came across information from outside, such as an article, a website, a technique, a talk, a product or a sight, and saw what it could mean for them.
codes.papers: Garud et al. (2011); Merton and Barber (2004); Shane (2000); + 3 more

codes.label: Unsought promotion by others (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: A person, outlet or platform promoted the product on its own initiative, such as a YouTuber's video, an influencer's post or a platform's feature, without the founder asking or offering anything.
codes.papers: No paper yet: an inductive code, from the interviews

anomaly.captures: Something unexpected started it, but no trigger code names that kind of event

level1.name: Background
level1.sq_text: What background (prior knowledge, a problem in mind, contacts) and which mechanisms (noticing, connecting, acting, changing plans) turn the trigger into an opportunity?
level1.asks: What did the founder already have?

codes.label: Relevant expertise
codes.captures: The founder's knowledge, training or experience in a field let them see the value of the unexpected event when others might not.
codes.papers: Cohen and Levinthal (1990); Merton and Barber (2004); Copeland et al. (2023); + 19 more

codes.label: A problem already in mind
codes.captures: Before the event, the founder was already carrying a specific problem, need or strong interest, and the chance input mattered because it connected to it.
codes.papers: Felin et al. (2021); Merton and Barber (2004); Copeland et al. (2023); + 2 more

codes.label: Idea grew from their work
codes.captures: The founder's job, daily tasks or hands-on experience gave them the closeness from which the idea came.
codes.papers: Wareham et al. (2022); von Hippel and von Krogh (2016); Shah and Tripsas (2007)

codes.label: Their network brought it
codes.captures: The unexpected opportunity, idea or information reached the founder through people they knew: friends, family, colleagues, communities.
codes.papers: Meyer and Skak (2002); Busch (2024); de Rond (2014); + 10 more

anomaly.captures: The founder brought something relevant that no background code covers

level1.name: Mechanism
level1.sq_text: What background (prior knowledge, a problem in mind, contacts) and which mechanisms (noticing, connecting, acting, changing plans) turn the trigger into an opportunity?
level1.asks: What did the founder do to turn it into something?

codes.label: Noticing it
codes.captures: The founder paid attention to something unexpected that others overlooked or would have dismissed.
codes.papers: Busch and Grimes (2023); Merton and Barber (2004); Brown (2005); + 6 more

codes.label: Connecting the dots
codes.captures: The founder linked the unexpected input to a need, problem, skill or piece of knowledge, and saw a new idea in the combination (Busch's 'association').
codes.papers: Smith and Hilbolling (2025); Copeland et al. (2023); Busch (2024); + 12 more

codes.label: Acting on it
codes.captures: The founder took concrete steps to pursue the unexpected event: followed up, invested time or money, built or launched something.
codes.papers: Reijonen and Heroum (2026); Copeland et al. (2023); Balzano (2022); + 13 more

codes.label: Changing the plan
codes.captures: The founder dropped or reshaped the original plan, product or goal to follow the unexpected input.
codes.papers: Murayama et al. (2015); Balzano (2022); Fultz and Hmieleski (2021); + 7 more

codes.label: Following what took off
codes.captures: The founder tried things in the market, watched how customers responded, and built on what unexpectedly worked.
codes.papers: Alvarez and Barney (2007); Eisenhardt and Sull (2001); Sarasvathy (2001); + 3 more

anomaly.captures: The founder did something with the event that no mechanism code covers

level1.name: Role
level1.sq_text: What role does it play in the venture (founding, redirecting, advancing it), and what outcomes follow: a product, a market, growth, or nothing?
level1.asks: What part did it play in the venture?

codes.label: Started the venture
codes.captures: The unexpected event gave rise to the business idea, the first project or first customer, or made founding possible.
codes.papers: Dew (2009); Balzano (2022); Copeland et al. (2023); + 8 more

codes.label: Accidental founder
codes.captures: The founder had no plan to start a business, or this business, and the unexpected event made them a founder.
codes.papers: Reijonen and Heroum (2026); Shah and Tripsas (2007); Engel et al. (2017); + 1 more

codes.label: Changed the venture's direction
codes.captures: The unexpected event made the venture turn from its original plan: a new product, market, customer or business model (a pivot).
codes.papers: Liu and de Rond (2016); Kirtley and O'Mahony (2023); Balzano (2022); + 18 more

codes.label: Moved the venture forward
codes.captures: After founding, the unexpected event brought growth: a big order, a key partner, press, a new market, without changing direction.
codes.papers: Meyer and Skak (2002); Brownell et al. (2024); Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017); + 2 more

anomaly.captures: It played a part in the venture other than starting, redirecting or advancing it

level1.name: Outcome
level1.sq_text: What role does it play in the venture (founding, redirecting, advancing it), and what outcomes follow: a product, a market, growth, or nothing?

codes.label: A new product or service
codes.captures: A specific product, service, feature or process came out of the unexpected event.
codes.papers: Busch (2024); Busch and Grimes (2023); Cunha et al. (2010); + 6 more

codes.label: A new market or opportunity
codes.captures: The event revealed a market, customer group, channel or opportunity the founder had not seen or planned for.
codes.papers: Balzano (2022); Graebner (2004); Smith and Hilbolling (2025); + 3 more

codes.label: Growth and results
codes.captures: The founder credits the unexpected event, and what they did with it, with growth, sales, revenue or profit.
codes.papers: Fultz and Hmieleski (2021); Balzano (2022); Oo et al. (2025); + 5 more

codes.label: Nothing came of it
codes.captures: The unexpected opportunity was missed, dismissed, dropped or forgotten.
codes.papers: Busch (2024); Smith and Hilbolling (2025); Cunha et al. (2010); + 6 more

codes.label: Harm or loss (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: The unexpected event cost the venture: lost sales, income or a channel, a costly mistake, or a threat to its survival.
codes.papers: Austin et al. (2012); Copeland et al. (2023); Cunha et al. (2015); + 2 more

codes.label: Resources, contacts or knowledge (added in 2.0)
codes.captures: What came of the unexpected event was something the founder could use later: a supplier, partner, funding or other resource, new contacts, or knowledge and ideas, rather than a product, a market or growth.
codes.papers: Busch and Barkema (2020); Klyver et al. (2025); Balzano (2022); + 6 more

anomaly.captures: A result that no outcome code covers

level1.name: Condition
level1.sq_text: Which conditions make it more or less likely to occur and be acted on: seeking out chance, cheap trials, loose plans, or scarce resources?
level1.asks: What made it easier or harder?

codes.label: Putting themselves in chance's way
codes.captures: The founder actively made unexpected opportunities more likely: going to events, talking to many people, trying many things, sharing their work.
codes.papers: Copeland et al. (2023); Eisenhardt and Sull (2001); Merton and Barber (2004); + 5 more

codes.label: Cheap to try
codes.captures: Trying the new idea cost little, so the founder could act on the unexpected without much risk.
codes.papers: Reijonen and Heroum (2026); Austin et al. (2012); Denrell et al. (2015); + 4 more

codes.label: No fixed plan
codes.captures: The founder held plans loosely, which left room to follow the unexpected; or held them rigidly, which nearly made them miss it.
codes.papers: Dew (2009); Balzano (2022); Merton and Barber (2004); + 7 more

codes.label: Little money or resources
codes.captures: Having little money or few resources pushed the founder to rely on what turned up and improvise.
codes.papers: Fultz and Hmieleski (2021); Busch and Grimes (2023); Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); + 4 more

anomaly.captures: A circumstance that made it easier or harder, not covered by a condition code

level1.name: Account
level1.sq_text: How do founders account for it afterwards: as luck, as luck plus effort, as clear only in hindsight, or retold as planned?
level1.asks: How does the founder tell it afterwards?

codes.label: Credited to luck
codes.captures: The founder explicitly explains an event or success as luck, chance or being in the right place at the right time.
codes.papers: Krumboltz (1998); Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); Oo et al. (2025); + 5 more

codes.label: Part luck, part effort
codes.captures: The founder divides credit between luck and their own skill or hard work.
codes.papers: Nair et al. (2020); Dew (2009); Oo et al. (2025); + 4 more

codes.label: Only clear in hindsight
codes.captures: The founder says the event seemed minor at the time and only later proved to be a turning point.
codes.papers: Otto et al. (2024); Engel et al. (2017); Graebner (2004); + 3 more

anomaly.captures: A way of telling it that no account code covers

rows.name: Busch (2024)
rows.rule: Agency: acted on it (1.5) AND Surprise (1.4) AND Value (1.6)
rows.papers: Busch (2024); Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); Klyver et al. (2025); + 3 more

rows.name: Dew (2009)
rows.rule: Surprise (1.4) AND Relevant expertise (3.1) AND (Open to any business (1.2) OR Searching for something specific (1.3))
rows.papers: Dew (2009); Busch (2024); Engel et al. (2017); + 3 more

rows.name: Walpole, after Merton and Barber (2004)
rows.papers: Merton and Barber (2004); Busch and Barkema (2020); Cunha et al. (2010); + 4 more

rows.name: Pure luck
rows.in_short: Surprise and value without agency (Busch 2024, p. 29)
rows.rule: Surprise (1.4) AND Value (1.6) AND NOT Agency: acted on it (1.5)
rows.papers: Busch (2024); Merton and Barber (2004); Copeland et al. (2023); + 11 more

rows.name: Targeted search or a plan
rows.in_short: Agency and value without surprise (Busch 2024, p. 29)
rows.rule: Searching for something specific (1.3) AND Agency: acted on it (1.5) AND Value (1.6) AND NOT Surprise (1.4)
rows.papers: Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); Bhave (1994); Kirzner (1997); + 20 more

rows.name: Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly
rows.in_short: A specific search, answered by the problem already in mind
rows.rule: Searching for something specific (1.3) AND A problem already in mind (3.2) AND NOT Changing the plan (4.4)
rows.papers: Yaqub (2018); Merton and Barber (2004); Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017); + 8 more

rows.name: Walpolian: sought one, found another
rows.in_short: A specific search that changed the plan
rows.rule: Searching for something specific (1.3) AND Changing the plan (4.4)
rows.papers: Yaqub (2018); Merton and Barber (2004); Mirvahedi and Morrish (2017); + 6 more

rows.name: Bushian: exploring, met an existing need
rows.in_short: No specific search, but a problem already in mind
rows.rule: A problem already in mind (3.2) AND (Not looking at all (1.1) OR Open to any business (1.2))

rows.name: Stephanian: solution first, problem later
rows.in_short: No specific search and no problem in mind
rows.rule: (Not looking at all (1.1) OR Open to any business (1.2)) AND NOT A problem already in mind (3.2)
rows.papers: Yaqub (2018); Balzano (2022); Fultz and Hmieleski (2025); + 1 more

rows.name: Told as if planned
rows.in_short: The story is told as intended, though its details show unplanned turns
rows.rule: Decided by the researchers, with a written reason
rows.papers: de Rond and Thietart (2007); Merton and Barber (2004); Van Lent et al. (2022); + 11 more

rows.name: Working with what's at hand
rows.in_short: Built from the founder's own means, with no surprise
rows.rule: Decided by the researchers, with a written reason
rows.papers: Reijonen and Heroum (2026); Cunha et al. (2010); Carayannis et al. (2011); + 4 more

new.captures: Relevant to the research question, but no group asks about it
